title: Photography direction for an education product
excerpt: Photograph the learning moment and caption the choice. A dashboard of badges is the team's mirror, not proof that someone learns.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a mood that still has to point at the lesson.
caption: A pale beach at sunrise, small waves and distant palm trees. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should education photography show?
faqs.answer: The learning moment, close enough to read the exercise or the teacher list. A sunny classroom with a blurry screen is context at most. It is not proof. Caption the choice in a line that would be false under a different picture.

faqs.question: Why not lead with badges?
faqs.answer: Because the picture wins, and badges answer the team's retention question rather than the buyer's. A parent wants to know if a child will practice. A teacher wants to know who is stuck. Trophies imply that comparison is the point.

faqs.question: Can you use a child's photo?
faqs.answer: Only with the permission your policy requires, and not because a pilot photo tested well. When you are unsure, export a demo account with fictional names and label it as the product. Stock children pointing at a blank screen do not solve this.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Education product website photography should show the learning moment. Reject a dashboard full of badges. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline.

A teacher or a parent with little time can feel warmed by a sunny classroom and still have no idea what the child will do. Warmth is not the product. The lesson is. The frame has to prove the lesson.

## The learning moment in the frame

Choose the sentence first. "A child reads one sentence and tries the next." "A teacher sees who is stuck before walking over." "A parent starts a short practice and does not have to teach it." Then choose the picture that makes that sentence true. If the picture could sit on any education homepage, it is not your moment.

The strongest frame is often the product itself. The exercise, cropped close enough to read a line of it. The hint after a wrong step. The short list of students on the same skill, with any real names removed. A marketing photograph of a laptop from across a room, with a blurry screen, throws away the only evidence you had. Get closer. Let the lesson be legible.

When you photograph a person, photograph the act. A parent looking at a phone that shows the practice, with the practice readable. A teacher glancing at a class view, with the view readable. Hands only, if faces of children are not something you can publish. The act matters more than a portrait. A child grinning at the camera is a different ad, the one every parent has already learned to distrust.

Context can be one frame, not the campaign. A kitchen table or a classroom tells the constraint, the ten minutes, the noisy period. It does not replace the screen. Sequence them: where this happens, then the moment, then stop. A dozen lifestyle images are a delay.

## Reject the badge dashboard

A dashboard of badges, streaks, and ranks photographs the team's anxiety about retention. It does not photograph learning. On a homepage it tells a parent that comparison is the point. It tells a teacher that the product will create a pecking order you then have to manage. If your pedagogy is quieter than that, your pictures cannot be louder.

Do not "balance" a badge wall with a caption about whole-child learning. The picture wins. People remember the trophies. If encouragement exists inside the product, show the encouragement that is a sentence after a hard step, not a chest of medals. The sentence is the learning moment. The chest is a game about using the app.

Charts of time-on-task have the same problem. They prove that the app was open. A teacher already knows how to waste a period. Show the step the student could do afterward, or the stuck list that helped the teacher intervene. Those are decisions. Minutes are not.

If a badge screen is honestly the product, then the product is a motivation layer and the site should say that. Do not show medals and talk about mastery. Pick one story and photograph it. Mixed stories are how a careful buyer decides you will mix them in the classroom too.

## Caption the picture

Write a caption that states what is in the frame and what choice it supports. "The practice after a missed word, with a hint that shows the sound, not a lost streak." A parent skimming on a phone may read the caption and not the essay. [Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people read only about a quarter of the text on a page. Spend the caption on the lesson.

Do not caption with "empowering every learner." That line can move to any competitor's photo. If the caption still works when the image is swapped for stock, both the caption and the image are unfinished. Rewrite until the words would be false under a different picture.

Keep captions short enough to sit under a phone crop. Two lines. The decision and the boundary if you need it. "Ten minutes, one skill, no timer." A paragraph under every image turns the page into a manual. One manual page can exist. The homepage cannot be five manuals.

Alt text is the caption's twin, not a keyword field. Describe the frame. "A phone on a table showing a one-sentence reading prompt and a place to try the next word." [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats that description as part of making the page perceivable. A person who does not see the image should still learn what the lesson is. "Student engaged with platform" teaches them nothing.

## What not to stage

Do not stage a diverse group of children pointing at a screen you cannot read. The diversity is not the problem. The empty screen is the problem, and the pointing is a cliché that hides it. Either get permission and show a real moment, or do not use children as props. A product crop is more respectful than a borrowed face.

Do not put a real student's work, name, or face on the marketing site because it tested well. Permission for a pilot is not permission for an ad. When you are unsure, use a demo account you created, with obviously fictional names, and label the frame as the product. Fictional is fine. Pretending fictional is a real child is not.

Do not grade every photo through a heavy warm filter so the brand "feels safe." Safety is in the lesson design, the privacy line, and the absence of public shame. A filter that makes the product illegible is working against the only thing the buyer came to see. Light, consistent treatment is enough. The lesson's own contrast has to survive.

Do not illustrate the skill with metaphors that insult the buyer. A child as a rocket. A brain as a lightbulb. A ladder to the stars. Teachers have seen the ladder. Show the fraction, the sentence, the word. Concrete beats inspirational, especially for an adult who has to trust you with a learner who is struggling.

Avoid stock that shows the wrong age. If you teach early reading, a photograph of teenagers in a lab is a different product. Age is part of the learning moment. Getting it wrong tells the buyer you do not know who the lesson is for, which is fatal on this page.

## A shot list you can finish

Write the list before the shoot or the export, and keep it small.

- One close frame of the learner's step, readable, from the real product.
- One frame of the adult view you actually sell, teacher or parent, with fictional data.
- One context frame only if the setting is the constraint.
- No badge wall, no handshake, no graduation caps, no floating screens in a void.
- A caption and an alt sentence written the same day, while the choice is still clear.

Export from the build when you can, at the crop the phone site will use. A desktop analytics view shrunk into a phone-shaped mockup is how the badge dashboard sneaks back. If the phone product is the real product for parents, photograph that.

Store the selects where the team can reuse them without grabbing an old trophy screenshot. On a Hanabi project, brand files live in the client portal with the docs and the updates. You need a home that is not a chat thread. The next page someone adds should obey the same shot list, or the site will grow a second, worse campaign beside the first.

Direction is the list plus the refusals. "Make parents feel something" is not direction. "Show the step, caption the choice, never lead with a badge" is direction. A new teammate can follow the second one.

## Pictures on the page that has to be fast

The hero image is in the first ten seconds. It has to load, and it has to be the lesson. A huge uncropped photograph of a classroom, plus a second image of the product, plus a background video, spends the parent's patience on weight. One sharp frame. A size reserved in the layout so the page does not jump. The rest of the story below, if you still need it.

Hanabi treats that restraint as part of the build: a marketing page that is fast before it is clever, with images that have a job. Your education page can do the same without a lecture about tools. If the picture is slow, it is the wrong picture, even when it is pretty.

Review the homepage with the images only, no paragraphs. Could a stranger say what the learner does? If they say "kids and computers," the direction has not started. Replace the frame. Do not add a paragraph to apologize for it.

The frame also has to survive the width of a phone, because that is where this buyer will judge you. [The mobile visit for an education product](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-an-education-product) is the next piece. The first screen still has to show the learning moment and a way to start a class or a trial. A crop that only works on a laptop will fail the visit you are most likely to get.

When you want the pictures held to the same standard as the interface, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice which frames carry a decision. Then cut any education image that would still "work" on a site that had no lesson.
